title: The Death of King Saul
overview: King Saul and three of his sons, including Jonathan, die in battle against the Philistines, and the people of one town risk a night march to give them a burial.

parts.label: Defeat on Mount Gilboa (vv. 1-3)
parts.note: The Philistines, Israel's longtime enemy, crush Israel's army on Mount Gilboa in the north, just as Saul had been warned the night before (chapter 28). Saul's sons die first, among them Jonathan, David's closest friend, and Saul himself is badly wounded by archers.

parts.label: Saul takes his own life (vv. 4-6)
parts.note: Saul begs his armor bearer to kill him rather than be captured and mocked by the "uncircumcised," an insult meaning foreigners outside Israel's covenant with God. When the terrified man refuses, Saul falls on his own sword, the armor bearer does the same, and the text plainly records that they all died that day.

parts.label: Israel's towns abandoned (v. 7)
parts.note: News of the defeat sends Israelites in the nearby valley and east of the Jordan River fleeing their towns, since conquered people often faced death or slavery. The Philistines simply move in and take them over.

parts.label: The bodies put on display (vv. 8-10)
parts.note: The Philistines behead Saul and send word of the victory to their temples, treating it as a win for their gods. His armor goes to a temple of Ashtoreth, a goddess they worshiped, and his body is hung on the wall of Beth Shan, a city near the Jordan, as public humiliation.

parts.label: Jabesh Gilead's night rescue (vv. 11-13)
parts.note: Early in his reign Saul had saved the town of Jabesh Gilead from a cruel enemy (chapter 11), and its fighters now repay him by marching through the night to take the bodies down. Burning bodies was not normal Israelite practice, and scholars are unsure why they did it, though it may have been to prevent further abuse; they then buried the bones under a tree and fasted seven days in mourning.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether this chapter mainly presents Saul's end as God's judgment on a disobedient king or as a tragedy told with sympathy for a broken man, and how to view his suicide follows from that.
think: When someone's life ends badly, what, if anything, do the people they once helped still owe them?
